title: Tower and antenna safety
blurb: How to climb, raise and ground a tower safely, and how far to keep from power lines.

T0B01.why: Keep lightning ground connections **short and direct**. A long or looping path adds impedance and slows the surge reaching ground.
T0B01.trap: Drip loops and right-angle bends work against a fast surge.

T0B02.why: Climbing requires training, a harness, and tie-off at all times: **all of them**.

T0B03.why: Always have a helper or observer. **Never** climb alone, whatever the height or the work.

T0B04.why: Look for and **stay clear of overhead electrical wires**. Contact can be fatal.
T0B04.trap: Grounding yourself or insulating the tower doesn't stop lightning or line contact.

T0B05.why: Vibration slowly turns a turnbuckle. A safety wire **prevents loosening** from vibration.
T0B05.trap: It isn't a lightning ground and it doesn't measure tension.

T0B06.why: Allow enough distance that if the antenna falls, **no part comes within 10 feet** of the power wires.
T0B06.trap: Wavelength and line height don't set the clearance: the fall zone does.

T0B07.why: Don't climb a crank-up tower unless it is **retracted** or **mechanical locking devices** are installed. It could collapse.
T0B07.trap: Crank-up towers should be grounded and may be painted.

T0B08.why: Use **separate 8-foot rods for each leg**, bonded to the tower and to each other.
T0B08.trap: One short rod, a choke or a water pipe isn't adequate.

T0B09.why: A utility pole carries high-voltage lines, so your antenna **could contact them**.

T0B10.why: Sharp bends add inductance that blocks a lightning surge. Keep the wire **short and smoothly bent**.

T0B11.why: **Local electrical codes** set grounding requirements for towers and antennas.
T0B11.trap: Part 97, the FAA and UL don't write the grounding rules.
